title: Event Triggered Execution: Trap
summary: The trap builtin in Unix shells registers a command list that the shell runs when it receives a specified signal. Signals are the operating system's way of telling a process that something happened, and the keyboard interrupt from control and C, the terminal end signal, and the shell exit signal are the ones users meet most often. Legitimate scripts use trap to clean up temporary files or shut down gracefully instead of dying in the middle of their work. The technique here is to register a handler that starts a malicious payload, so the trigger is a signal rather than a login, a file type, or a startup entry. Because a trap only exists inside a running shell, an attacker must also arrange for the trap to be set again in each new session, which is where this sub-technique leans on its parent: the trap line is typically hidden in a shell startup or logout file so that every new shell registers the handler before anything else runs. Detection artefacts are therefore shared with the parent, and the distinguishing detail is the handler text itself. Commands that decode, fetch, or run content, and signal handlers that fire on shell exit, are worth reviewing, as are startup files whose timestamps do not match their apparent purpose.

beginner.definition: A signal is a short message that the operating system sends to a program, for example when you press control and C to stop it. The shell has a built-in command called trap that lets you say what to do when a signal arrives. This technique is when an attacker uses it to run their own code.
beginner.whyItMatters: The attacker's code waits quietly and runs only when the chosen signal arrives. The signal is normal, so the activity fits the everyday use of the machine. Because the trap lives in the shell itself, it can also be set up again in every new session. This makes the code hard to notice in a list of processes.
howItWorks: The attacker writes a trap line that names the command to run when a signal arrives.
They choose a common signal, such as the one sent by pressing control and C.
Because a trap only lasts as long as the shell, they hide the line in a shell startup file.
Every new shell then registers the handler again before you type anything.
The handler may start a program, fetch something, or clean up traces on the way out.
Some attackers use the signal sent when a shell exits, so the code runs after the session ends.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel night desk with a standing instruction: if a guest rings the bell, also open the service corridor. Nothing happens while the desk is quiet. Someone replaces the instruction card so that the bell now unlocks a staff room instead. Only the guests who ring the bell ever set it off.
takeaways: A trap is a shell rule that decides what happens when a signal arrives.
The trap itself does not survive on its own, so look for how it is set again.
Signal handlers in startup files that fetch or run commands deserve a careful read.

objectives: Explain what a signal is and why programs handle signals.
Describe how the shell trap command registers a signal handler.
Explain why a trap must be reloaded to survive across sessions.
Explain how the trap command relates to shell startup file persistence.
Identify the artefacts that reveal a malicious signal handler.
